sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today we come to one of the greatest rescue stories ever told: Moses and the Exodus. The word exodus means a going out, or departure. It's the story of how God brought the people of Israel out of slavery in Egypt and made them His own nation.

By this time, Joseph's family had lived in Egypt for about four hundred years and had grown into a great multitude. But a new Pharaoh arose who did not know Joseph. As you listen, notice how God hears the cries of people who are suffering, and how He uses an unlikely, unwilling man to carry out His plan.

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
The new Pharaoh was afraid of the Israelites because there were so many of them. So he made them slaves and forced them to build cities with brick and mortar. When that didn't stop them from growing, he gave a terrible command: every Hebrew baby boy was to be thrown into the river.

One Hebrew mother hid her baby son for three months. When she couldn't hide him any longer, she made a little ark of bulrushes, covered it with pitch, laid the baby inside, and placed it among the reeds at the river's edge. His sister watched from a distance. Pharaoh's own daughter came down to bathe, saw the basket, and heard the baby crying. She had compassion on him. His sister bravely stepped forward and offered to find a Hebrew nurse — and she brought the baby's own mother! The child grew up in Pharaoh's palace, and Pharaoh's daughter named him Moses.

When Moses was grown, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave, and in anger he killed the Egyptian. When it became known, Moses fled to the land of Midian. There he married, became a shepherd, and lived for forty years.

Then one day, near Horeb, the mountain of God, Moses saw something strange: a bush that was burning, yet was not consumed. When he turned aside to look, God called to him out of the bush: “Moses, Moses.” And God said, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry.” He told Moses that He was sending him to Pharaoh to bring His people out.

Moses made excuse after excuse. Who am I? What if they don't believe me? I am not eloquent. Please send someone else. God answered, “Certainly I will be with thee.” When Moses asked God's name, Exodus chapter three, verse fourteen gives God's answer: “And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.” God also sent Moses' brother Aaron to speak with him.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh with God's message. Exodus chapter five, verse one: “Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness.” But Pharaoh answered, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?” Instead of letting them go, he made their work even harder.

So God sent plagues upon Egypt — ten of them. The river turned to blood. Then came frogs, lice, and swarms of flies. The livestock died. Boils broke out on people and animals. Hail destroyed the crops, locusts ate what was left, and a thick darkness covered the land for three days. Again and again, Pharaoh promised to let the people go, and again and again he hardened his heart.

Then God announced the tenth and final plague: the firstborn in every Egyptian home would die. But God gave Israel a way of escape. Each family was to kill a lamb without blemish and put its blood on the doorposts of their house. Exodus chapter twelve, verse thirteen: “and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt.” This was the first Passover. That night there was a great cry in Egypt, and Pharaoh finally told Moses to take the people and go.

But soon Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them with his chariots. The Israelites were trapped between the Red Sea and the Egyptian army, and they were terrified. Moses told them, “Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD.” Exodus chapter fourteen, verse twenty-one: “And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.” Israel walked through on dry ground. When the Egyptians followed, the waters returned and covered them. On the other side, Moses and Miriam led the people in songs of praise.

In the wilderness, God fed His people with manna from heaven and water from a rock. And at Mount Sinai, God gave them the Ten Commandments, beginning with: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me.”

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What does this story teach us?

First, God sees and hears those who are suffering. He told Moses, I have seen, and I have heard their cry. If you are hurting today, God is not distant from your pain.

Second, God uses ordinary, imperfect people. Moses had a past he was ashamed of, and he felt completely unqualified. But God's answer to every excuse was simply, I will be with you. God doesn't need us to be impressive; He needs us to be willing.

Third, God is more powerful than any Pharaoh. Whatever seems to hold you captive — fear, addiction, guilt, or a situation you can't escape — God is able to make a way where there seems to be no way, just as He did at the Red Sea.

And finally, the Passover points us to Jesus. The New Testament calls Jesus “our passover” who was “sacrificed for us.” Just as the blood of the lamb protected Israel, the sacrifice of Jesus covers all who trust in Him, and brings us out of slavery to sin into new life with God.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Think about your own “Red Sea” — a situation where you feel trapped. Hear Moses' words: stand still, and see the salvation of the Lord.

Let's pray. Lord God, thank You that You see and hear me. Thank You that You are greater than anything that holds me captive. When I feel unqualified, remind me that You are with me. Thank You for Jesus, the Lamb whose sacrifice sets me free. In His name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll hear how a young shepherd named David faced a giant.
